::: {.objectives}
**Goals.** Fit a resource selection function and a step selection function to
the same fisher; interpret both with relative selection strength; recover the
realised movement kernel; test whether habitat changes how the animal moves;
and find out which method recovers a **known** selection coefficient from a
simulated animal.

**Time:** ~70 minutes. **Packages:** `amt`, `terra`, `survival`, `dplyr`,
`ggplot2`.
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(amt)
library(terra)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)
```
:::


## The data: fishers in New York

`amt` ships GPS tracks of four fishers (*Pekania pennanti*) from LaPoint et al.
(2013), with three rasters: land use (GlobCover, 300 m), elevation, and human
population density.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
data(amt_fisher)
amt_fisher |> count(name)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>   name        n
#>   <chr>   <int>
#> 1 Leroy     919
#> 2 Lucile   1349
#> 3 Lupe     3004
#> 4 Ricky T  8958

cov <- get_amt_fisher_covars()

# GlobCover classes 40-100 and 160-170 are forest
forest <- cov$landuse %in% c(40:100, 160:170)
covs <- c(forest,
          resample(cov$elevation, forest),
          resample(cov$popden, forest))
names(covs) <- c("forest", "elevation", "popden")
covs
#> class       : SpatRaster
#> size        : 54, 59, 3  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
#> resolution  : 220, 302  (x, y)
#> extent      : 1775801, 1788781, 2398484, 2414792  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
#> coord. ref. : +proj=aea +lat_0=23 +lon_0=-96 +lat_1=29.5 +lat_2=45.5 +x_0=0 +y_0=0 +datum=NAD83 +units=m +no_defs
#> source(s)   : memory
#> names       : forest,  elevation,      popden
#> min values  :  FALSE,  49.067795,   23.639465
#> max values  :   TRUE, 147.865814, 4051.015869
```
:::


We work with **Lupe**, sampled every ~2 minutes, resampled to a regular
10-minute interval.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
lupe <- amt_fisher |>
  filter(name == "Lupe") |>
  track_resample(rate = minutes(10), tolerance = minutes(2)) |>
  filter_min_n_burst(min_n = 3)

nrow(lupe)
#> [1] 774
```
:::


## Task 1 — A resource selection function

Used locations versus random points within Lupe's range (third order).


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(1)
rsf_dat <- lupe |>
  random_points(n = nrow(lupe) * 10) |>
  extract_covariates(covs) |>
  mutate(forest = factor(forest, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("other", "forest")),
         elevation_z = as.numeric(scale(elevation)),
         popden_z    = as.numeric(scale(popden)),
         w = ifelse(case_, 1, 5000))

rsf <- glm(case_ ~ forest + elevation_z + popden_z,
           data = rsf_dat, family = binomial(), weights = w)
round(summary(rsf)$coefficients, 3)
#>              Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
#> (Intercept)   -12.428      0.577 -21.524    0.000
#> forestforest    1.601      0.579   2.767    0.006
#> elevation_z     0.245      0.035   6.965    0.000
#> popden_z       -0.108      0.037  -2.889    0.004
```
:::


### Your turn

**1a.** Express each coefficient as relative selection strength with a 95% CI.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
b  <- coef(rsf)[-1]
se <- summary(rsf)$coefficients[-1, 2]
data.frame(term = names(b), RSS = round(exp(b), 2),
           lower = round(exp(b - 1.96 * se), 2), upper = round(exp(b + 1.96 * se), 2))
#>                      term  RSS lower upper
#> forestforest forestforest 4.96  1.60 15.42
#> elevation_z   elevation_z 1.28  1.19  1.37
#> popden_z         popden_z 0.90  0.83  0.97
```
:::


Relative to what is available within her range, Lupe's locations are several
times more likely to fall in forest than in other cover, more likely at higher
elevation (per standard deviation), and less likely where people are dense.
The intercept is meaningless — it depends only on how many available points
you drew.
:::

## Task 2 — The same fisher, as a step selection function


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(2)
ssf_dat <- lupe |>
  steps_by_burst() |>
  random_steps(n_control = 10) |>
  extract_covariates(covs, where = "both") |>
  mutate(forest_end   = factor(forest_end,   levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("other", "forest")),
         forest_start = factor(forest_start, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("other", "forest")))

ssf_dat |> select(step_id_, case_, sl_, ta_, forest_end, elevation_end) |> head(11)
#> # A tibble: 11 × 6
#>    step_id_ case_   sl_    ta_ forest_end elevation_end
#>  *    <dbl> <lgl> <dbl>  <dbl> <fct>              <dbl>
#>  1        3 TRUE   99.7  0.216 forest             105. 
#>  2        3 FALSE  42.9  2.87  forest             105. 
#>  3        3 FALSE 172.  -2.70  forest              98.9
#>  4        3 FALSE 132.  -1.59  forest              97.9
#>  5        3 FALSE  54.7 -0.242 forest             105. 
#>  6        3 FALSE  19.5 -1.22  forest             105. 
#>  7        3 FALSE 210.  -1.84  forest              97.8
#>  8        3 FALSE  72.2 -0.979 forest             105. 
#>  9        3 FALSE  86.5 -1.59  forest              97.9
#> 10        3 FALSE 353.  -0.341 forest              99.6
#> 11        3 FALSE  11.3 -0.199 forest             105.
```
:::


One **stratum**: the step Lupe took (`case_ = TRUE`) and ten she could have
taken from the same point at the same moment.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
issf <- fit_issf(ssf_dat,
                 case_ ~ forest_end + elevation_end + popden_end +
                   sl_ + log(sl_) + cos(ta_) + strata(step_id_),
                 model = TRUE)
round(summary(issf$model)$coefficients[, c(1, 3, 5)], 4)
#>                     coef se(coef) Pr(>|z|)
#> forest_endforest  1.4803   0.7378   0.0448
#> elevation_end     0.0679   0.0196   0.0005
#> popden_end       -0.0010   0.0008   0.2009
#> sl_              -0.0001   0.0005   0.8262
#> log(sl_)          0.0684   0.0629   0.2771
#> cos(ta_)          0.0361   0.0670   0.5895
```
:::


### Your turn

**2a.** Compute the RSS for a step ending in forest versus other cover, with a
confidence interval, using `log_rss()`.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x1 <- data.frame(forest_end = factor("forest", levels = c("other", "forest")),
                 elevation_end = mean(ssf_dat$elevation_end, na.rm = TRUE),
                 popden_end    = mean(ssf_dat$popden_end, na.rm = TRUE),
                 sl_ = 100, ta_ = 0)
x2 <- x1
x2$forest_end <- factor("other", levels = c("other", "forest"))

rss <- log_rss(issf, x1, x2, ci = "se")
exp(rss$df[, c("log_rss", "lwr", "upr")])
#>   log_rss      lwr      upr
#> 1 4.39433 1.034846 18.65991
```
:::


Given two equally reachable destinations, identical in elevation and
population density, Lupe is roughly four times as likely to step into forest.
The interval is wide: forest covers most of this landscape, so there are few
strata where forest and non-forest are both on offer — a reminder that
selection can only be estimated where there is **choice**.
:::

## Task 3 — The realised movement kernel

The control steps were drawn from a *tentative* gamma and von Mises fitted to
the observed steps. The movement terms in the model correct them.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
upd_sl <- update_gamma(sl_distr(ssf_dat),
                       beta_sl = coef(issf)[["sl_"]],
                       beta_log_sl = coef(issf)[["log(sl_)"]])
upd_ta <- update_vonmises(ta_distr(ssf_dat), beta_cos_ta = coef(issf)[["cos(ta_)"]])

data.frame(
  quantity  = c("mean step (m)", "von Mises kappa"),
  tentative = round(c(prod(unlist(sl_distr(ssf_dat)$params)), ta_distr(ssf_dat)$params$kappa), 2),
  realised  = round(c(prod(unlist(upd_sl$params)), upd_ta$params$kappa), 2)
)
#>          quantity tentative realised
#> 1   mean step (m)    147.26   154.38
#> 2 von Mises kappa      0.34     0.38
```
:::


::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Reading it

Here the two kernels are close, and the movement coefficients are not
significant: once selection is accounted for, Lupe's movement is well
described by the distributions the controls were drawn from. When they differ,
the realised kernel is the one to use for prediction or simulation — it is the
animal's movement with the habitat effect removed.
:::

## Task 4 — Does habitat change how she moves?

Interact the movement terms with the habitat at the **start** of the step.
First the obvious candidate, forest:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
issf_forest <- fit_issf(ssf_dat,
                        case_ ~ forest_end + elevation_end + popden_end +
                          sl_ + log(sl_) + cos(ta_) +
                          sl_:forest_start + cos(ta_):forest_start +
                          strata(step_id_),
                        model = TRUE)
round(summary(issf_forest$model)$coefficients[, c(1, 2, 5)], 3)
#>                                coef    exp(coef) Pr(>|z|)
#> forest_endforest              1.284 3.611000e+00    0.079
#> elevation_end                 0.067 1.070000e+00    0.001
#> popden_end                   -0.001 9.990000e-01    0.209
#> sl_                           0.105 1.111000e+00    0.994
#> log(sl_)                      0.069 1.072000e+00    0.271
#> cos(ta_)                     25.751 1.525347e+11    0.993
#> sl_:forest_startforest       -0.106 9.000000e-01    0.994
#> cos(ta_):forest_startforest -25.721 0.000000e+00    0.993
```
:::


### Your turn

**4a.** Look at the standard errors of the two interaction terms. What went
wrong?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

Standard errors in the tens or thousands mean the model **cannot estimate**
those terms. Count the information:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ssf_dat |> filter(case_) |> count(forest_start)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>   forest_start     n
#>   <fct>        <int>
#> 1 other            2
#> 2 forest         519
```
:::


Almost every observed step starts in forest. With a couple of non-forest
starts, there is nothing to compare: the likelihood is flat and the optimiser
wanders off towards infinity (quasi-complete separation). The coefficient is
not "huge"; it is undefined.

Always check that the covariate you interact with **varies** among observed
steps before you interpret an interaction.
:::

Population density does vary. Standardise it and interact it with both step
terms (they define the gamma distribution together):


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ssf_dat <- ssf_dat |> mutate(pop_start_z = as.numeric(scale(popden_start)))

issf_pop <- fit_issf(ssf_dat,
                     case_ ~ forest_end + elevation_end + popden_end +
                       sl_ + log(sl_) + cos(ta_) +
                       sl_:pop_start_z + log(sl_):pop_start_z +
                       strata(step_id_),
                     model = TRUE)
round(summary(issf_pop$model)$coefficients[, c(1, 3, 5)], 4)
#>                         coef se(coef) Pr(>|z|)
#> forest_endforest      1.4758   0.7385   0.0457
#> elevation_end         0.0677   0.0195   0.0005
#> popden_end           -0.0010   0.0008   0.2014
#> sl_                  -0.0003   0.0006   0.5710
#> log(sl_)              0.0848   0.0647   0.1901
#> cos(ta_)              0.0358   0.0670   0.5935
#> sl_:pop_start_z      -0.0015   0.0007   0.0270
#> log(sl_):pop_start_z  0.1174   0.0757   0.1209
```
:::


**4b.** The two interaction terms work together. Translate them into Lupe's
mean step length where population density is low (−1 SD) and high (+1 SD).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
b <- coef(issf_pop)
kernel_at <- function(z) {
  g <- update_gamma(sl_distr(ssf_dat),
                    beta_sl     = b[["sl_"]]      + z * b[["sl_:pop_start_z"]],
                    beta_log_sl = b[["log(sl_)"]] + z * b[["log(sl_):pop_start_z"]])
  data.frame(popden_start_sd = z, mean_step_m = round(g$params$shape * g$params$scale))
}
bind_rows(lapply(c(-1, 0, 1), kernel_at))
#>   popden_start_sd mean_step_m
#> 1              -1         170
#> 2               0         152
#> 3               1         141
```
:::


Where more people live, Lupe takes shorter steps — she moves more slowly
through the populated parts of her range. The effect is modest, and one animal
is one animal; but this is exactly the kind of **habitat-mediated movement**
an RSF cannot express and an iSSA can.

Always interpret step-length interactions through the implied distribution,
never from one coefficient: `sl_` and `log(sl_)` change the scale and shape
together, and only their combination has a meaning.
:::

## Task 5 — Is there enough contrast?

A step selection function can only detect selection for a covariate that
**varies within one step's reach**. The land-use raster has 300 m cells.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
same_cell <- cellFromXY(covs, cbind(ssf_dat$x1_, ssf_dat$y1_)) ==
             cellFromXY(covs, cbind(ssf_dat$x2_, ssf_dat$y2_))
c(median_step_m = median(ssf_dat$sl_[ssf_dat$case_]),
  share_in_start_cell = round(mean(same_cell, na.rm = TRUE), 2))
#>       median_step_m share_in_start_cell 
#>            128.3752              0.4800
```
:::


::: {.callout-important}
## Match covariate grain to step length

About half the control steps never leave the cell they started in: for those
strata the land-use value is identical for the used step and its alternatives,
and they carry no information about forest selection. Elevation, on a much
finer grid, is estimated far more precisely. When covariates are coarser than
your steps, either get finer covariates or ask a coarser question — never
"solve" it by quietly making the steps longer.
:::

## Task 6 — Ground truth: which method recovers a known coefficient?

`R/simulators.R` contains `simulate_ssf()`: an animal that moves with a fixed
kernel and, at each step, **chooses** among 30 possible next steps with
probability proportional to $\exp(\beta \times \text{habitat})$. That is
exactly the process an SSF assumes. We set $\beta = 1.5$.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
source("R/simulators.R")
hab <- simulate_habitat()                         # a smooth, standardised habitat surface
sim <- simulate_ssf(1500, hab, beta = 1.5, start = c(0, 0))
sim$t <- as.POSIXct("2026-01-01", tz = "UTC") + (sim$step - 1) * 600
sim_trk <- make_track(sim, x, y, t)
```
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(hab, col = hcl.colors(50, "Greens", rev = TRUE), main = "Simulated habitat and animal")
lines(sim$x, sim$y, col = "firebrick", lwd = 0.8)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){fig-align='center' width=576}
:::
:::


### Your turn

**6a.** Fit an SSF and an RSF to the simulated animal. Which recovers
$\beta = 1.5$? **6b.** Repeat with $\beta = 0$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
compare_methods <- function(beta) {
  s <- simulate_ssf(1500, hab, beta = beta, start = c(0, 0))
  s$t <- as.POSIXct("2026-01-01", tz = "UTC") + (s$step - 1) * 600
  tr <- make_track(s, x, y, t)
  set.seed(3)
  ssf <- tr |> steps() |> random_steps(n_control = 15) |> extract_covariates(hab, where = "end")
  m_ssf <- fit_issf(ssf, case_ ~ habitat + sl_ + log(sl_) + cos(ta_) + strata(step_id_), model = TRUE)
  rsf <- tr |> random_points(n = nrow(tr) * 10) |> extract_covariates(hab) |>
    mutate(w = ifelse(case_, 1, 5000))
  m_rsf <- glm(case_ ~ habitat, data = rsf, family = binomial(), weights = w)
  data.frame(true_beta = beta,
             SSF = round(coef(m_ssf)[["habitat"]], 2),
             SSF_se = round(sqrt(diag(vcov(m_ssf$model)))[["habitat"]], 2),
             RSF = round(coef(m_rsf)[["habitat"]], 2),
             RSF_se = round(summary(m_rsf)$coefficients["habitat", 2], 2))
}
bind_rows(compare_methods(1.5), compare_methods(0))
#>   true_beta   SSF SSF_se   RSF RSF_se
#> 1       1.5  1.42   0.11  1.02   0.03
#> 2       0.0 -0.04   0.09 -0.06   0.03
```
:::


The **SSF recovers the true coefficient** (within its standard error) because
it is fitted to the same process that generated the data: each step compared
with its own reachable alternatives.

The **RSF does not**, and it is not supposed to. It compares locations with
everywhere in the range, as if the animal could teleport; the answer mixes
selection with the constraint of having to walk. Note also its standard error:
three to four times *smaller* than the SSF's, for a *less* accurate estimate.
The RSF treats 1,500 autocorrelated positions as independent, so it is
confidently wrong.

That is not an argument against RSFs — for broad-scale questions about where
ranges sit they are the right tool. It is an argument for knowing which
question each method answers, and simulation with a known truth is how you
find out.
:::

## To hand in

::: {.callout-tip}
## Weekly submission

Fit the iSSA of Task 2 to a **second** fisher (Leroy, Lucile or Ricky T). Report
the RSS for forest with its CI and one paragraph comparing it with Lupe's. Is
the difference biological, or could it come from how much choice each animal
had (Task 5)?
:::

## Self-check

::: {.quiz}
Removing `strata(step_id_)` from an SSF formula:

- [ ] Only changes the standard errors
- [x] Fits a different, wrong model: every step is compared with every control step in the dataset
- [ ] Speeds up fitting without changing the estimates
- [ ] Turns the SSF into an RSF with the same meaning

::: {.quiz-feedback}
The stratum is the design: each used step is compared only with the
alternatives from the same place and time. Without it, a step in the forest at
dawn is compared with control steps from the other side of the range days
later — the local, time-specific availability that made the SSF worth fitting
is gone.
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
An RSF gives a smaller standard error than an SSF for the same animal. Does
that make it more reliable?

- [ ] Yes — smaller standard errors mean more precise estimates
- [x] No — the RSF treats autocorrelated fixes as independent, so its precision is overstated
- [ ] Yes, if the RSF has more available points
- [ ] Only if the two coefficients agree

::: {.quiz-feedback}
In the ground-truth task the RSF's standard error was several times smaller
and its estimate further from the truth. Precision you did not earn is worse
than honest uncertainty: it makes a wrong answer look certain.
:::
:::
